questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically examine the healing of the man at the pool in John Chapter 5.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** John 5:1-18 tells of Jesus healing a man at a pool in Jerusalem during a Jewish feast. It is one of the signs of the Fourth Gospel and leads to a long discourse on the authority of the Son.

**1. The setting.** The pool, called Bethesda (or Bethzatha) in the manuscripts, was by the Sheep Gate and had five porticoes where many sick people lay. Some manuscripts add an explanation that an angel stirred the water; the earliest ones do not, so it is uncertain. The man had been ill for thirty-eight years.

**2. The healing.** Jesus takes the initiative and asks, "Do you want to be made well?" The man answers that he has no one to put him into the pool. Jesus says, "Stand up, take your mat and walk", and he is healed at once. The man is cured by the word of Jesus, not by the pool, which shows Jesus' power over illness and his care for the helpless.

**3. The Sabbath conflict.** It was the Sabbath, and the Jewish authorities objected to the man carrying his mat. When Jesus finds the man in the Temple, he says, "Do not sin any more, so that nothing worse happens to you" (5:14), a warning that does not necessarily mean that sickness is always caused by sin. The man reports Jesus to the authorities, and they begin to persecute Jesus.

**4. The claim of Jesus.** Jesus says, "My Father is still working, and I also am working" (5:17). This makes his critics seek to kill him, because he was breaking the Sabbath and calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God. The discourse that follows says that the Son gives life and judges, and that he is witnessed to by the Father, John the Baptist, his works and the Scriptures (5:19-47).

**5. Critical comments.** The man's apparent lack of response, and his informing the authorities, have been read as ingratitude or simply fear. The story is less about the details of the cure than about its meaning: Jesus gives life, breaks the limits of Sabbath interpretation, and reveals his relation to the Father. The healing, like other signs, calls for faith and divides people.

**Conclusion.** The healing at the pool shows compassion and divine authority, and also introduces the opposition that will end in the cross.
